units.title: Why async
units.blurb: Waiting vs. working, Task as a promise of a result, and the big reveal: while I/O is in flight, no thread is needed.

lessons.title: Waiting is the enemy
lessons.sub: Why a window goes "Not Responding"

cards.title: A waiter by the stove
cards.body:
Picture a waiter who takes an order and then stands by the stove until the dish is ready. Every other table waits.

That is synchronous code: the thread waits for the network or the disk and does nothing else. A good waiter hands the order to the kitchen and goes to serve other tables. That is asynchrony.

cards.title: Why the window freezes
cards.body:
An app with a window (WPF, WinForms, Unity) has one main thread, also called the UI thread. It draws the UI and handles clicks.

The main thread runs a message loop: it takes an event from the queue (a click, "repaint the window"), handles it, and takes the next one. Until the click handler returns, nobody picks up the next event.

If the handler is waiting for a server, the window stops responding: clicks pile up in the queue and nobody is there to handle them.

cards.task: Run the synchronous version to the end. On which tick is the user's click handled? You won't need the "thread pool" row in this lesson; the pool is covered in the next one.

cards.title: What await changes
cards.body:
Compare two handlers. In the synchronous one, the thread reaches the network call and stands there until the reply arrives.

In the asynchronous one, GetDataAsync sends the request and immediately returns a Task<string>, a "claim ticket" for a future string (more on that in the next lesson). await sees that there is no reply yet and returns control: the main thread goes back to working through the queue (clicks, repaints).

The word async in front of a method allows await inside it (more in u2).

The key point: await doesn't stand and wait. It leaves and comes back later.

cards.title: Continuation and context
cards.body:
When the reply arrives, the rest of the handler (Show(r)) is put into that same message queue and runs on the main thread. That rest is called the continuation.

await remembers where it was called from (in a window, the main thread) and sends the continuation back there. That "where" is called the context; we'll take it apart in u4.

Step by step:
1. A click: the main thread calls OnClick, and the request goes out.
2. await sees there is no reply yet, and the handler returns control.
3. The main thread handles other events: clicks, repaints.
4. The reply arrives: the continuation is put into the main thread's queue.
5. The thread gets to it and runs Show(r).

cards.task: Now switch the handler to await and run it to the end. When is the click handled, and where does the continuation run?

cards.q: The user clicked while the server request was in flight. Why was the click handled almost at once with await, but only after the reply without it?
options: While we wait for the network, the main thread is free to work through the message queue
await makes the network faster
Another thread handles the click
cards.explain: await returns control for the duration of the wait, and the message loop picks up the next click. The network is no faster; the thread just isn't sitting idle. Without await the handler holds the thread until the reply arrives.

cards.q: Click handler: async void OnClick() { var r = await GetDataAsync(); Show(r); }. The server reply has arrived. Which thread runs Show(r)?
options: The main (UI) thread: the continuation is put into its queue
The thread that was waiting for the server reply
A new thread created by await
cards.explain: No thread was waiting for the reply: the main thread was handling clicks meanwhile. When the reply arrived, the continuation Show(r) was put into the main thread's queue, because that is where await was called.

cards.title: I/O vs. computation
cards.body:
There are two very different things you can wait for.

I/O: network, disk, database. The hardware does the work, and the thread just waits.
Computation (CPU): compression, physics, parsing. The processor itself does the work, and the thread is genuinely busy.

async/await is mainly about the first kind: how not to hold a thread while you wait.
cards.code:
string text = await File.ReadAllTextAsync(path); // waiting for disk: thread is free
byte[] zip = Compress(bytes);                    // CPU is computing: thread is busy

cards.q: Which of these are I/O waits? Select all that apply.
options: An HTTP request
Reading a file from disk
A database query
Compressing an image
Running physics
cards.explain: Compression and physics are CPU work. You can move them to another thread, but there is nothing to wait for.

cards.q: Does async/await make the server request itself faster?
options: No: the request takes just as long, but the thread isn't idle
Yes, twice as fast
Yes, if the server supports async
cards.explain: The win is that the thread does other work meanwhile: drawing the window or serving other clients.

cards.q: Where is a blocked main thread most noticeable?
options: In a windowed app or a game: the picture freezes
In a console tool
Nowhere, you can't see it
cards.explain: At 60 frames per second a game has just 16 ms per frame. Any wait on the main thread is a freeze.

lessons.title: Task: a promise of a result
lessons.sub: A claim ticket instead of the answer

cards.title: A Task is a claim ticket
cards.body:
A Task is an object meaning "work that will finish later". Think of a dry cleaner's ticket: your clothes aren't ready yet, but you hold a slip you'll trade for them later.

A Task<string> is a ticket you'll trade for a string.

cards.title: Get the ticket, collect later
cards.body:
There are two ways to collect the result.

await t: if the task isn't done yet, the method releases the thread and resumes when the result appears (that's the continuation from the previous lesson).

t.Result: the thread stands and waits, like the waiter by the stove. On the UI thread that is the same freeze as a synchronous call, and sometimes a permanent one (we'll get to that in u4).

A task ends in one of three ways: success (with a result), an error (the Faulted state), or cancellation (Canceled). Until then it is in progress.
cards.code:
Task<string> t = http.GetStringAsync(url); // request sent, ticket in hand
DoOtherWork();                              // free to do something else
string html = await t;                      // thread is free while we wait
// string html = t.Result;                  // thread stands still while we wait
cards.deep: TaskStatus: Created, WaitingForActivation, WaitingToRun, Running, WaitingForChildrenToComplete, RanToCompletion, Canceled, Faulted. Tasks from async methods and I/O are usually WaitingForActivation: they aren't "running" on any thread, and something outside will complete them.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: The same, with an int result

cards.q: A method returned Task<string>. Where is the string?
options: It may not exist yet: await hands it over when the task completes
Inside the Task right away
In the Task.Text property
cards.explain: A task is a promise. The result appears when the operation finishes.

cards.q: How can a task end? Select all that apply.
options: Successfully, with a result
With an error (Faulted)
Canceled
Paused until the next run
cards.explain: Those are the three final states. You can't pause a task.

cards.title: The thread pool
cards.body:
Creating a thread for every small piece of work is expensive: each thread has its own stack (on the order of a megabyte), and the OS spends time creating it and switching between threads.

So .NET has a thread pool: a few pre-created background threads and a shared work queue. Right away the pool is ready to give you roughly as many threads as the CPU has cores.

Task.Run(f) puts f into the pool's queue and immediately returns a Task. A free pool thread takes the work and runs it; when f finishes, the task completes.

If all threads are busy, the work waits in the queue. The pool will add a thread eventually, but not right away. Remember this: in u4.l5 it becomes a problem.
flow: a free pool thread runs f

cards.title: Task.Run is for computation
cards.body:
Heavy computation inside a handler occupies the UI thread, and the window freezes. Task.Run moves it to the pool. Step by step:

1. The UI thread writes "Compressing…".
2. Task.Run puts Compress into the pool's queue and returns an incomplete task.
3. await sees the task isn't done, and the handler returns control: the window responds to clicks.
4. A pool thread finishes compressing, and the task completes.
5. The rest of the handler is put into the UI thread's queue and runs there, so it may touch Status.

Why await in a window comes back to the UI thread specifically is covered in detail in u4.l1. I/O doesn't need Task.Run: GetStringAsync already doesn't hold a thread.
cards.deep: Task.Run(async () => …) unwraps the inner task correctly. Task.Factory.StartNew with an async lambda returns Task<Task>: the outer task completes as soon as the lambda reaches its first real pause and returns the inner task. await waits only for that, not for the whole job. A classic mistake.

cards.q: You need to compress a large image without freezing the window. What do you do?
options: await Task.Run(() => Compress(img))
Call Compress(img) directly in the handler
Task.Run(() => Compress(img)).Result
cards.explain: Compress is CPU work. Calling it directly in the handler occupies the UI thread, and the window stops responding. Task.Run moves the work to the pool, and the handler releases the UI thread at await. After compression, the rest runs on the UI thread again.

wrong.1: Compression takes over the UI thread: the message loop stops until Compress finishes.
wrong.2: The pool does the compressing, but the UI thread stands on .Result until it's done, so the window freezes just the same.

cards.q: Should you wrap http.GetStringAsync(url) in Task.Run?
options: No: the request doesn't hold a thread anyway; Task.Run only adds a hop to the pool
Yes, or it will block the window
Yes, it's faster
cards.explain: GetStringAsync sends the request and returns a task right away; no thread waits on the network. Task.Run only adds a trip through the pool's queue and back.
cards.deep: The exception is "async" APIs that do noticeable synchronous work before their first real pause: for example, the old HttpWebRequest in .NET Framework could resolve DNS and detect proxies synchronously, and some database drivers behave similarly. For those, Task.Run in a UI app is sometimes justified, but only profiling tells you so.

cards.q: Get the result without blocking the thread
cards.code: string html = ___ http.GetStringAsync(url);
cards.explain: await "unwraps" a Task<string> into a string.

lessons.title: There is no thread
lessons.sub: Where is the thread during a request? Nowhere

cards.title: Where is the thread during a request?
cards.body:
Answer: nowhere. Let's walk through two lines step by step.

1. The thread calls GetStringAsync: it builds the request, hands it to the OS (a socket), and returns an incomplete Task.
2. await sees the incomplete task, remembers the continuation (the WriteLine line), and returns control. The thread is free.
3. Data travels over the network; the network card and the OS kernel receive it. No .NET thread is standing on this request.
4. The reply arrives: the OS notifies .NET, the task completes, and the continuation is queued: in a console app to the pool's queue, in a window to the UI thread's queue.
5. A free thread picks up the continuation and runs WriteLine.

The OS notifications come from its async I/O mechanisms: IOCP on Windows, epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS. A few .NET service threads wait for notifications for all of the process's operations at once, not one thread per request.

This is the famous "There is no thread", the title of an article by Stephen Cleary.
cards.code:
var html = await http.GetStringAsync(url);
Console.WriteLine(html.Length);
cards.deep:
Strictly speaking, without a context the continuation often runs right on the pool thread that handled the OS notification, with no separate trip through the queue. That's an implementation detail; the principle is the same.

A caveat about files. On Linux and macOS, .NET has no truly asynchronous file reads: FileStream.ReadAsync performs an ordinary blocking read on a pool thread. "There is no thread" is strictly true for sockets (network, a database over the network) and for files on Windows opened in asynchronous mode (File.ReadAllTextAsync opens them that way).

cards.task: A console program awaits a reply. Step through the ticks and watch the "network" row: is any thread busy while we wait? Who runs the continuation afterwards?

cards.q: 1,000 requests are awaiting replies. How many threads are blocked, each on its own request?
options: None: a few service threads wait for notifications for all the requests at once
One per core, the other requests wait in a queue
cards.explain: The OS waits for the requests, and the service threads wait for its notifications for all operations at once. A thread is needed only when there is code to run: sending the request, and later running the continuation.

cards.task: Compare on the thread pool: add 16 requests with await and watch the thread count and wait time. Then try .Result if you like: when all threads are busy, the pool adds a new one, but not right away.

cards.q: Why can an async server handle more requests?
options: While requests wait on the database and network, threads serve other requests
Async code compiles faster
The server gets more cores
cards.explain: Same number of threads, but none of them sits idle waiting.

cards.q: Does async speed up heavy computation?
options: Not by itself: computation still occupies a thread; you can only move it to the pool with Task.Run
Yes, async parallelizes the code
Yes, if you add await
cards.explain: async is about waiting, and computation has nothing to wait for. Task.Run doesn't make the calculation faster; it only moves it from the UI thread to a pool thread.

cards.q: Match them up
Put in order what happens on await http.GetStringAsync(url) in a console app
items: GetStringAsync sends the request and returns an incomplete task
await sees the incomplete task and returns control
The reply arrives: the OS notifies .NET, and the task completes
The continuation is put into the pool's queue
A free pool thread runs the continuation
cards.explain: A thread is involved only at the start and at the end. Between the second and third steps the OS waits for the request, not a thread.

lessons.title: Final: why async
lessons.sub: Waiting, Task and the thread that isn't there

cards.task: Make the window handle the user's click by tick 2 at the latest.

cards.q: What does the thread do while await waits for the server?
options: Other work, or nothing if there is none
Waits for the reply
Polls the network every millisecond
cards.explain: The OS waits, not the thread.

cards.q: Where does Task.Run make sense? Select all that apply.
options: Heavy computation started from the UI thread
Compressing a large file in memory
Wrapping http.GetStringAsync
Wrapping File.ReadAllTextAsync
cards.explain: Async I/O doesn't need Task.Run.

cards.q: What has Task<int> LoadAsync() returned while the request is still running?
options: An incomplete task
The number 0
null
cards.explain: The result comes later; you can wait for the task with await.

cards.q: How is await different from .Result?
options: await doesn't block the thread, .Result does
No difference
.Result is faster
cards.explain: Both wait for the result, but .Result holds the thread the whole time.

cards.q: The path of an async request: put it in order
items: The method sends the request and returns an incomplete task
await returns control, the thread is free
The reply arrives, the task completes
The continuation is queued
A free thread runs the continuation
cards.explain: A thread is needed at the start and at the end; while the request is in flight, the OS waits for it.

cards.q: A game makes a synchronous HTTP request on the main thread. What does the player see?
options: The picture freezes until the server replies
Nothing
A black screen forever
cards.explain: The main thread can't draw frames while it waits.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: No thread is busy while waiting

units.title: async and await in action
units.blurb: Your first async method, what to return, where exceptions go, WhenAll and WhenAny, and cancellation with CancellationToken.

lessons.title: Your first async method
lessons.sub: async, await and where a method pauses

cards.title: Two words
cards.body:
async in front of a method allows await inside it and changes what return means: the method is declared as Task<int> but returns an int. The compiler creates the task, and return puts the result into it.

Step by step:

1. The method runs like an ordinary one, synchronously, up to the first await.
2. GetStringAsync returned an incomplete task. await "pauses" the method, and the caller immediately gets an incomplete Task<int>.
3. The reply arrives, and the method continues from the line after await.
4. return html.Length completes that very task with the number, and the caller's await receives it.

cards.title: The start is synchronous
cards.body:
Up to the first await that actually waits, an async method runs like an ordinary one: on the calling thread, with no switching. Look at the output order: A, B, C.

Task.Delay(100) is a task that completes after 100 ms without occupying a thread (a timer completes it). The method pauses on it and returns its task, which is why B is printed before C.

If the task is already complete (await Task.CompletedTask, an answer from a cache), await checks that and moves on without pausing, on the same thread. And an async method with no await at all has no pauses: it runs to the end and returns an already completed task. How exactly await checks for completion is covered in u3.

cards.q: What does the caller get when GetLengthAsync reaches await on an incomplete request?
options: An incomplete Task<int>
A number
null
Nothing: the caller will wait
cards.explain: The method returns the task right away, at its first real pause. The result comes later.

cards.q: On which line can the method pause?
cards.explain: A pause can only happen at await.

cards.q: return html.Length returns an int, yet the method is declared as Task<int>. Why is that allowed?
options: The compiler created the task, and return puts the result into it
It's a compile error
An int automatically becomes a Task
cards.explain: In an async method, return sets the result of the future task, the one the caller received at the first pause.

cards.q: Make the method asynchronous
cards.explain: async in the declaration, await in front of the task.

cards.task: The same async code. Run it in the console to the end, then switch to WPF and run it to the end again. Who ran the continuation each time?

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: Up to the first await, an async method runs synchronously
await on an already completed task doesn't pause the method
An async method with no await inside runs synchronously
async by itself creates a new thread
await blocks the thread
cards.explain: async creates no threads and doesn't block. It's a way of cutting a method into pieces around the waits.

cards.q: What does the program print? Put the lines in output order.
items: start
before await
call returned
after await
end
cards.explain: WorkAsync prints "before await" synchronously, inside the call. At Task.Delay the method pauses and returns its task, so "call returned" comes before "after await". await t waits for the continuation, and only then comes "end".

lessons.title: What to return
lessons.sub: Task, ValueTask and the dangerous async void

cards.title: Task, Task<T>, ValueTask<T>
cards.body:
Task: no result, but you can wait for it. Task<T>: returns a T.

Task is a class: every task is a heap object that the GC later cleans up. ValueTask<T> is a struct with two modes: inside it holds either a ready T value (no heap object) or a reference to a real task (or to a reusable IValueTaskSource) when the result isn't there yet.

It pays off only when the result is often ready right away and the method is called very often. The price is a set of rules: a ValueTask is awaited exactly once, never from two places at the same time, and you don't read .Result before it completes. The reason is the reusable source: it may not support blocking waits, and after completion it may already be serving another operation. Need more? .AsTask() turns it into an ordinary task.

cards.title: async void is only for event handlers
cards.body:
You can't wait for an async void method: the caller never learns when it has finished.

Exceptions take a different path too. In an async Task method, the exception is stored in the task and is thrown to whoever awaits it. An async void method has no task, so the exception has nowhere to go and is thrown "into the air": in a window, into the UI thread's queue (none of your try blocks catch it there, and by default the app crashes); in a console app or on a server, onto a pool thread, which takes the process down. A try/catch around the call won't help: by the time the exception is thrown, the call has already returned.

Use async void only where an event dictates the signature: button.Click += async (s, e) => …

cards.q: Why is async void dangerous?
options: You can't wait for it, and you can't catch its exception with a try around the call
It's slower
It can't use await
cards.explain: No task means nothing to wait for and nothing to carry the exception.

cards.q: A console app: try { SendAsync(); } catch (IOException) { Log(); }, where async void SendAsync() throws IOException after an await. What happens?
options: The catch doesn't fire: the exception is thrown later on a pool thread and crashes the process
The catch catches the IOException
The exception quietly stays inside the SendAsync task
cards.explain: SendAsync returned at its first await, so the try is already behind us. async void has no task, so the exception is thrown onto a pool thread, and nobody catches it there.

cards.q: Which line is a design mistake?
cards.explain: SaveAsync isn't an event handler; it needs async Task so it can be awaited.

cards.q: When is ValueTask<T> better than Task<T>?
options: When the result is often ready right away and the method is called very often
Always
When the method waits a long time for the network
cards.explain: The savings are only on the fast path with no waiting. If the method always waits, there is an ordinary task inside anyway, and the difference is negligible.

cards.q: What must you not do with a ValueTask? Select all that apply.
options: Await it twice
Await it from two places at once
Read .Result before it completes
Await it once
cards.explain: After completion, the source inside a ValueTask may already belong to another operation. If you need to wait more than once, call .AsTask() and work with an ordinary task.
cards.deep: IValueTaskSource is reused to get zero allocations even on the slow path: for example, Socket in .NET keeps one such source for reads and one for writes and hands them out again and again. A repeated await of such a ValueTask will, at best, throw InvalidOperationException (the source checks the operation number, the token); with a source that doesn't check, it gets the result of someone else's operation.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: No allocation if ready right away

cards.q: Fix the signature
cards.explain: async Task is a method with no result that can be awaited.

lessons.title: Exceptions
lessons.sub: await, .Result and AggregateException

cards.title: await throws like ordinary code
cards.body: If a task faulted, await throws its exception, the very one thrown inside. You catch it with an ordinary try/catch around the await.

cards.title: An error before the first await
cards.body:
In an async method every exception goes into the task, even one thrown before the first await, for example by an argument check. It doesn't come out of the call itself; it shows up where the task is awaited.

An ordinary method that returns a Task without the async keyword would throw such an exception straight out of the call.

cards.q: Where is the ArgumentNullException thrown?
options: At await t
At the SendAsync(null) call
Nowhere: the exception stays in the task, and await doesn't throw it
cards.explain: The method is marked async, so the exception from the check went into the task. The call returned an already faulted task, DoOtherWork ran, and await t threw the exception.

cards.title: .Result and .Wait() wrap
cards.body:
If you wait synchronously with .Result or .Wait(), the exception arrives wrapped in an AggregateException, with the original inside, in the InnerExceptions list.

Why the difference? .Result and .Wait() are APIs from .NET 4 (the TPL library), where a task can have several errors: for example, a task that waits for several others at once (next lesson). So they always throw a wrapper with a list. await was designed for code that looks synchronous: it throws the first exception from the list, with its original type and original stack trace (via ExceptionDispatchInfo).

GetAwaiter().GetResult() throws the original exception, like await, but still blocks the thread. It's the very method await calls under the hood (we'll take it apart in u3).

cards.q: Will this catch handle the network error?
cards.code:
try { var r = GetAsync().Result; }
catch (HttpRequestException) { … }
options: No: .Result throws AggregateException, with the HttpRequestException inside
Yes
Only in Release
cards.explain: One more reason not to block: the thread stands still, and exceptions arrive wrapped (and in a window, .Result also risks a permanent hang, u4).

cards.title: Forgotten exceptions
cards.body:
If nobody awaits a task, nobody sees its exception. Since .NET 4.5 the app doesn't crash because of it; the error is simply lost.

The last chance to notice it is the TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException event. But it fires not when the error happens, but when the GC collects the task and its finalizer notices the unobserved exception. That may happen in seconds, in minutes, or never.

That's why "fire and forget" hides errors. The reliable way not to lose them is to catch them inside the task itself (more in u5).

cards.q: A faulted task was started and never awaited. When does TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException fire?
options: When the GC collects the task: maybe in minutes, maybe never
Right when the error happens
When the method that started the task returns
cards.explain: The unobserved exception is noticed by the task's finalizer, which runs only after a garbage collection. You can't rely on this event for logging.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: await throws the original exception
.Result wraps it in AggregateException
An exception before the first await in an async method is thrown at the await of its task, not at the call
An exception from a task nobody awaited crashes the app immediately
try/catch doesn't work with await
cards.explain: With await, try/catch works just like with synchronous code. And since .NET 4.5 the error of a task nobody awaited doesn't crash the app; it is lost.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: The original, but the thread is blocked
The error of a task nobody awaited

lessons.title: Several tasks at once
lessons.sub: One by one, WhenAll and WhenAny

cards.title: One by one or together
cards.body:
A task starts at the moment the method is called: GetProfileAsync() sends the request right away and hands back a Task, and await only waits. So "start them together" means call all the methods first, then wait.

You can await three independent requests one by one: await, await, await. The times add up, because the next method is called only after the previous reply.

Or you can call all three at once and wait for them together with Task.WhenAll(…), a task that completes when all the tasks passed to it have completed. The time is that of the slowest request. If you pass tasks with a result, Task<T>, await WhenAll returns a T[] array in argument order.
cards.deep: Lazy Select. In var tasks = urls.Select(u => http.GetStringAsync(u)); no request has gone out yet: Select only describes a sequence. The requests start when WhenAll enumerates it. If you enumerate tasks again (say, tasks.Count() or a second WhenAll), the requests go out again. That's why people write .ToArray() or .ToList().

cards.task: Three requests: 300, 500 and 200 ms. Get the total time down to 500 ms or less.

cards.q: Three requests of 300, 500 and 200 ms are awaited one by one. How long does it all take?
options: 500 ms
300 ms
cards.explain: 300 + 500 + 200. Each next method is called, and so its request starts, only after the previous reply.

cards.task: Go back to "one by one" and make the first request fail. What happened to the others?

cards.q: With sequential awaits, why did requests B and C never even start after A failed?
options: await A threw, and execution never reached the lines with B and C
WhenAll canceled them
The server refused everyone
cards.explain: An exception stops the method at the very first await. GetOrdersAsync and GetBalanceAsync were never called, so their requests never started.

cards.title: WhenAll and errors
cards.body:
The WhenAll task completes only when all the tasks passed to it have completed, even if one of them failed right away.

If several failed, the WhenAll task ends faulted, and its Exception.InnerExceptions holds all the errors, in argument order, not in the order they happened. await throws the first one from that list (as in the previous lesson). To see them all, keep the WhenAll task in a variable.

cards.task: Switch to Task.WhenAll and make A and C fail (C, at 200 ms, fails before A). What does await throw, and what is stored in the WhenAll task?

cards.q: await Task.WhenAll(tA, tB, tC): A failed (at 300 ms) and C failed (at 200 ms, earlier). What does await throw?
options: Only A's exception, the first in argument order
Only C's exception, since it happened first
An AggregateException with both
cards.explain: The errors in the WhenAll task are in argument order, and await throws the first one from the list: A's exception, even though C failed earlier. All the errors are in the WhenAll task's Exception.InnerExceptions. .Result and .Wait() would throw an AggregateException, not await.

cards.title: WhenAny: who's first
cards.body:
Task.WhenAny returns a task that completes when the first of the given tasks completes, and its result is the winning task itself. Hence the double await: the first gets the winner, the second gets its result.

The winner is the first task to complete, including one that failed. WhenAny itself doesn't throw: the exception surfaces when you await the winner. The other tasks keep running, so you should cancel them with a token (next lesson).

The second example is a timeout: the work races against Task.Delay.

cards.q: You need data from whichever of three mirrors is fastest. What do you use?
options: Task.WhenAny
Task.WhenAll
Sequential await
cards.explain: WhenAny completes together with the fastest mirror. The other requests should be canceled with a token so they don't waste resources.

cards.q: The requests still go one by one. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: The await inside the loop waits for each reply before the loop calls the next GetStringAsync. Remove that line: all the calls go out at once, and WhenAll waits for them all.

cards.q: Start all the requests at once
cards.code:
var tasks = urls.Select(u => http.GetStringAsync(u)).ToArray();
string[] pages = await Task.___(tasks);
cards.explain: Every GetStringAsync is called before the waiting starts, so all the requests have gone out at once. WhenAll waits for all of them and returns the results array in url order.

lessons.title: Cancellation and timeouts
lessons.sub: CancellationToken: a polite request to stop

cards.title: Cancellation is a request
cards.body:
Cancellation in .NET is cooperative: a CancellationTokenSource hands out a token (CancellationToken), you pass it to methods, and they check it themselves and stop working. You can't forcibly "kill" a task.

A source can be created with a timeout: new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)) cancels its token by itself after 5 seconds. To cancel manually, call cts.Cancel().

A method that notices cancellation throws OperationCanceledException. The async method's task then goes into the Canceled state (not Faulted), and awaiting that task throws OperationCanceledException again. HttpClient throws its subclass, TaskCanceledException, so catch (OperationCanceledException) catches it too.

cards.q: The server didn't reply within 5 seconds. What happens?
cards.code:
using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
var data = await http.GetStringAsync(url, cts.Token);
options: The token is canceled, and await throws TaskCanceledException, a subclass of OperationCanceledException
The request keeps waiting
The program exits
cards.explain: After 5 seconds the source cancels the token by itself. HttpClient, which received the token, aborts the request, its task becomes Canceled, and await throws TaskCanceledException, a subclass of OperationCanceledException.

cards.title: Your own code must listen to the token too
cards.body:
cts.Cancel() only sets a flag in the token and calls its subscribers. Code finds out about cancellation at the next check: ThrowIfCancellationRequested() throws OperationCanceledException, and HttpClient, the file API or a database driver that received the token abort the operation themselves.

So in a long loop, check the token between steps and pass it on to every async method. Otherwise cancellation gets stuck at your method.

Methods receive the token, not the source: the receiver can only listen, and only the owner of the CancellationTokenSource can cancel.

cards.q: An import loop: cts.Cancel() is called while the synchronous Parse(text) is running. When does the method stop?
options: When Parse finishes: at the next ThrowIfCancellationRequested check
Immediately, right inside Parse
Never: cancellation is noticed only at the start of a method
cards.explain: Cancel only sets a flag. Parse doesn't check the token, so it runs to the end, and on the next iteration ThrowIfCancellationRequested throws OperationCanceledException.

cards.q: Where does cancellation get lost?
cards.explain: SaveAsync didn't get the token: a save in progress won't be interrupted.

cards.title: When a method doesn't take a token
cards.body:
You can't stop someone else's operation without a token; you can only stop waiting for it.

task.WaitAsync(ct) and task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan) (.NET 6+) return a task that completes together with the original one, or earlier: with OperationCanceledException on the token, or with TimeoutException on the timeout.

The operation itself keeps running in the background, and nobody will see its result or its error.
cards.code:
var t = legacy.DownloadAsync(url);                       // takes no token
var data = await t.WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));   // TimeoutException after 5 s

cards.q: How do you cancel a task that doesn't accept a token?
options: Not directly: you can only stop waiting for it, e.g. with WaitAsync(token)
Call task.Abort()
Set task = null
cards.explain: WaitAsync stops the waiting, but the operation itself keeps running in the background. A Task has no way to stop someone else's code from the outside.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: Cancellation is cooperative
Cancellation usually throws OperationCanceledException
A CancellationTokenSource can be created with a timeout
Cancel() stops any code instantly
Checking the token at the end of the method is enough
cards.explain: Code stops only where it checks the token. A check at the end of the method is useless: the work is already done by then.

cards.q: Pass cancellation down
cards.code: await SaveAsync(item, ___);
cards.explain: Methods receive the token itself, not the source: only its owner should cancel.

units.blurb: What the compiler turns an async method into: the state machine, the awaiter, the fast path and ValueTask, ExecutionContext and AsyncLocal.

lessons.title: The awaiter pattern
lessons.sub: What the compiler turns every await into

cards.title: await x is four calls
cards.body:
The compiler doesn't know the word "task". When it sees await x, it expands it into the calls shown below:

  • x.GetAwaiter() gets the waiting object, the awaiter;
  • awaiter.IsCompleted asks whether it's already done;
  • if not, awaiter.OnCompleted(continuation) says "call me when it's ready". The method returns and the thread is free;
  • once it's ready, awaiter.GetResult() takes the result or throws the exception.

The compiler looks up GetAwaiter, IsCompleted and GetResult by name, with no interface involved, and GetAwaiter may even be an extension method. The awaiter itself, however, must implement the INotifyCompletion interface, which declares OnCompleted. Task awaiters also implement ICriticalNotifyCompletion with its UnsafeOnCompleted method, and that's what the generated code subscribes through (in the next lesson you'll see it as AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted).

cards.q: Match each awaiter-pattern member to its role
pairs: What to call when it's done
Take the result or the exception

cards.q: Rebuild what await expands into
cards.explain: First the awaiter, then the readiness check. Subscribing happens only if it isn't ready.

cards.q: What must an awaiter type implement for the compiler to accept await?
options: The INotifyCompletion interface with its OnCompleted method
Nothing: all awaiter methods are looked up by name only
It must derive from TaskAwaiter
cards.explain: GetAwaiter, IsCompleted and GetResult are looked up by name. Subscribing to completion goes through the INotifyCompletion interface. TaskAwaiter is a struct, so nothing can derive from it.

cards.title: Your own awaitable in two lines
cards.body: Since GetAwaiter is looked up by name, you can add it to someone else's type as an extension method. For example, to TimeSpan: have it return the awaiter of a Task.Delay task, and you can await a span of time directly.

cards.q: Why did await TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1) compile?
options: TimeSpan has a GetAwaiter extension method, and it returns the TaskAwaiter of a Task.Delay task
TimeSpan derives from Task
await can wait on any type without extra code
cards.explain: The compiler looks for GetAwaiter the same way foreach looks for GetEnumerator, so an extension method counts. The TaskAwaiter of the Task.Delay task does the rest.

cards.title: GetResult and exceptions
cards.body:
A faulted task keeps its exceptions as a list inside an AggregateException. .Result hands you the whole wrapper. A task awaiter's GetResult() behaves differently: it throws the first exception in the list and keeps its original stack trace.

It is GetResult that throws the exception after an await. That's why after await you catch the FormatException itself, not an AggregateException. You can call the same GetResult without await too: t.GetAwaiter().GetResult().
cards.code:
Task<int> t = ParseAsync("x");      // the task faulted with FormatException
int a = t.Result;                    // AggregateException with FormatException inside
int b = t.GetAwaiter().GetResult();  // FormatException itself, original stack
int c = await t;                     // same as GetResult

cards.q: A task faulted with FormatException. What does its awaiter.GetResult() do?
options: Throws the FormatException itself with its original stack
Throws an AggregateException with the FormatException inside
Returns default and records the error in the task
cards.explain: .Result throws the AggregateException wrapper. GetResult (and therefore await) throws the task's first exception as is.

cards.title: Task.Yield: a guaranteed pause
cards.body:
Task.Yield() returns an awaitable whose awaiter always answers IsCompleted = false. So await is guaranteed to suspend the method, and the continuation is queued: in a window, to the UI thread's queue; in a console app, to the thread pool.

Why: to hand the caller a Task right now and run the rest of the method later. Note that Yield doesn't move work to the background. In a window the UI thread still runs the rest, just a bit later. For background work you need Task.Run.
cards.deep: In WPF the continuation after Yield goes to the Dispatcher queue with a priority higher than input, so a loop like while (…) { Work(); await Task.Yield(); } doesn't make the window responsive. In Unity the continuation queue is drained once per frame, and anything queued while it is being drained waits for the next frame. So a Yield loop there runs roughly one iteration per frame, but the exact moment depends on the frame phase; to wait for a frame, Unity has its own tools (see the Unity unit).

cards.q: What can you await? Select all that apply.
options: Task
ValueTask
Task.Yield()
A TimeSpan with a GetAwaiter extension method written for it
An int with no GetAwaiter of its own
cards.explain: Everything except int has a GetAwaiter, either its own or an extension method. await needs nothing more.

cards.q: Why write await Task.Yield()?
options: To guarantee the method suspends: the caller gets a Task immediately and the rest runs later from the queue
To wait 1 ms
To move the rest of the method to a background thread, even in a WPF window
cards.explain: Yield's awaiter always answers IsCompleted = false. In a window the same UI thread runs the rest, just later: Task.Run gives you a background thread, Yield doesn't.

lessons.title: The state machine
lessons.sub: What the compiler folds all of a method's awaits into

cards.title: await isn't magic, it's a switch
cards.body:
The compiler rewrites an async method into a struct: a state machine. Local variables become its fields, the method body becomes a MoveNext function, and the step number lives in a state field.

Every await is a spot where MoveNext can return and later come back: on the next call, a switch on state jumps to where it stopped.

Next to it sits the builder (AsyncTaskMethodBuilder<T>), a helper that creates the method's task and completes it.

cards.title: What happens on the call
cards.body:
The compiler turns SumAsync itself into a short "launcher" (code below). Step by step:

  • 1. The struct is created with state = -1, meaning "just started".
  • 2. builder.Start calls the first MoveNext right away, synchronously, on the caller's thread. That's why a method runs like an ordinary one up to its first await.
  • 3. MoveNext hits an awaiter that isn't done: it writes the step number to state, subscribes itself through builder.AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted (which uses the awaiter's UnsafeOnCompleted inside) and returns.
  • 4. SumAsync returns builder.Task, a task that isn't complete yet.
  • 5. The GetAAsync task completes and calls MoveNext again. The switch on state jumps to the right spot.
  • 6. At the end builder.SetResult(a + b) completes the task. If an exception was thrown, it's builder.SetException.

cards.task: The responses are still on their way. Step through MoveNext and count the calls and pauses.

cards.q: A method has two awaits, and neither task is ready yet. How many times is MoveNext called?
cards.explain: builder.Start makes the first call, then there's one more for each continuation after an await.

cards.q: Why isn't variable a lost between MoveNext calls?
options: It became a field of the state machine
The thread that started the method keeps it
The garbage collector saves it
cards.explain: The stack frame disappears between MoveNext calls, but the struct's fields stay. The thread has nothing to do with it: a different thread may run the continuation.

cards.q: Who calls MoveNext the first time, and on which thread?
options: builder.Start, synchronously, on the thread that called the method
The thread pool, right after the method is called
The GetAAsync task, when it completes
cards.explain: The first MoveNext runs right inside the method call. The GetAAsync task calls MoveNext the second time, after the pause.

cards.task: Turn on "Results are ready" and walk through again.

cards.q: By the time of the await, both tasks, GetAAsync and GetBAsync, have already completed. How many pauses and MoveNext calls are there?
options: 0 pauses, 1 MoveNext call
2 pauses, 3 MoveNext calls
0 pauses, 3 MoveNext calls
cards.explain: IsCompleted = true, so the subscribe branch is skipped and the method runs straight through in the first MoveNext call, the one builder.Start made.

cards.title: On the stack, then on the heap
cards.body:
In Release the state machine is a struct and lives on the stack as long as the method hasn't suspended. At the first real pause the builder moves it to the heap: it copies the struct into a "box" object. The box outlives the method's return, and MoveNext is later called on it.

Since .NET Core 2.1 that box is the method's task itself: AsyncStateMachineBox derives from Task<T>. So a pause usually costs a single allocation: the machine and the task are one object.
cards.deep: In Debug the state machine is a class rather than a struct, so that Edit and Continue works. That's why you measure async allocations only in Release.

cards.q: MoveNext hit an awaiter that isn't done. Put its actions in order.
items: Checks IsCompleted
Writes the step number to state
Subscribes MoveNext to completion via builder.AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted
Returns control
cards.explain: state is written before subscribing: the continuation may start on another thread right after the subscription, and the switch must see the correct step number.

Runs a piece of the method up to the next await

lessons.title: Fast path and allocations
lessons.sub: When await costs nothing, and what still lands on the heap

cards.title: Already done? No pause
cards.body:
If the awaited task has already completed (a cache hit, data already in a buffer), its awaiter answers IsCompleted = true. Then, inside MoveNext:

  • 1. the subscribe branch is skipped: state isn't written and there's no return;
  • 2. GetResult is called right away and hands over the ready result;
  • 3. the same MoveNext call keeps going to the next await.

No subscription, no leaving the method, no thread switch, and the state machine stays on the stack. This is the fast path.

cards.task: The results are already ready. Walk the fast path and watch the if (!awaiter.IsCompleted) line: does MoveNext ever reach the return inside it?

cards.q: A handler called SumAsync, and both tasks inside have already completed. Which thread runs return a + b?
options: The one that called SumAsync: the method ran straight through in the first MoveNext call
A pool thread
Whichever thread once completed the GetBAsync task
cards.explain: There were no pauses, so there are no continuations either: builder.Start ran the whole method on the caller's thread.

cards.title: Where allocations hide
cards.body:
A pause usually costs one allocation: the state machine moves to the heap, and that box is the task itself (previous lesson).

The fast path keeps the machine on the stack. But the caller still needs a task object, and the result has to live somewhere. So an async Task<int> that returned 1000 without a single pause still creates a new Task<int>.

The exception is values for which .NET keeps ready-made completed tasks: true and false, ints from −1 to 8, and the default value (null, 0, 0.0…). Task.FromResult(x) gives you the same completed task with result x by hand, and in modern .NET it uses the same cache: for 5 or null it returns a shared object, for 1000 a new one.
cards.code:
Task<int>  a = CountAsync();       // returned 1000 without a pause → a new Task<int>
Task<int>  b = CountAsync();       // and another one: ReferenceEquals(a, b) == false
Task<bool> c = CheckAsync();       // returned true → a shared completed task from the cache
Task<int>  d = Task.FromResult(5); // 5 is within −1…8 → also from the cache

cards.title: No allocations at all
cards.body:
These create no heap objects at all:

  • Task.CompletedTask, a single shared completed task with no result;
  • an async Task with no result that finished without a pause: the builder hands out that same shared task;
  • an async Task<T> that returned a cached value (true, false, −1…8, default);
  • a ValueTask<T> with a ready value: it's a struct, and the result lives right inside it.
cards.code:
// the method finished without a single pause: what landed on the heap?
async Task           SaveAsync()  { … }  // nothing: the shared completed task
async Task<bool>     CheckAsync() { … }  // nothing: tasks for true/false exist in advance
async Task<int>      CountAsync() { … }  // returned 1000 → a new Task<int>
async ValueTask<int> PeekAsync()  { … }  // nothing: the result is in the struct itself

cards.q: async Task<int> CountAsync() found the value in a cache and returned 1000 without a single pause. What ended up on the heap?
options: Only a Task<int> object holding the result; the state machine stayed on the stack
Nothing: without a pause an async method allocates no memory
Both the state machine and a Task<int>
cards.explain: The machine moves to the heap only on a pause. But the caller needs a task with result 1000, and there's no ready-made one in the cache.

cards.q: What creates no new heap objects? Select all that apply.
options: return Task.CompletedTask
new ValueTask<int>(42)
await on an already completed task
An async Task<int> that returned 1000 without a pause
An async method that suspended
cards.explain: CompletedTask is a shared object, ValueTask is a struct, and awaiting a finished task takes the fast path. A Task<int> holding 1000 is a new object, and a pause puts the machine on the heap.

cards.q: A method reads a cache, and the data is there 99% of the time. What should it return so that a cache hit allocates nothing?
options: ValueTask<T>: on a cache hit the result lives in the struct
async Task<T>: since the await doesn't pause, there are no allocations anyway
Task<T> via Task.Run
cards.explain: async Task<T> creates a new Task<T> on every hit (except for cached values). A ValueTask<T> with a ready value doesn't touch the heap.

cards.q: Which line is the allocation-free fast path?
cards.explain: A ValueTask with a ready value is a struct, so the heap isn't touched. The last line wraps the real LoadUserAsync task.

cards.title: The price of ValueTask
cards.body:
ValueTask pays for the savings with rules. It's single-use: behind it there may be an object that gets reused for another operation after the first await. So you await a ValueTask exactly once and never from two places at the same time. If you need more, turn it into an ordinary task first with .AsTask().

Hence the rule of thumb: Task<T> by default. ValueTask when the method is called very often, usually completes right away, and the profiler has shown the allocations.
cards.deep: Since .NET 6 you can mark a method with [AsyncMethodBuilder(typeof(PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder<>))], and then even a ValueTask method that suspends takes its objects from a pool. Turn it on selectively and after measuring.

cards.q: Can you await the same ValueTask twice?
options: No: the behavior is undefined; if you need it more than once, call .AsTask() first
Yes, just like a Task
Yes, but only in Release
cards.explain: A ValueTask is single-use: there may be a reused object behind it. Only a Task can be awaited many times.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A shared completed task with no result
A completed task with a result
No allocation on the fast path

lessons.title: Builder and ExecutionContext
lessons.sub: How the task learns about an exception, and what travels across await

cards.title: The exception goes into the task
cards.body:
The generated MoveNext is wrapped in try/catch. If an exception is thrown inside, the catch doesn't rethrow it but calls builder.SetException(ex), and the task moves to the Faulted state. The exception "rides" inside the task until someone awaits it: await (that is, GetResult) throws it again.

A consequence: even an exception before the first await doesn't escape the call of a Task-returning method. The first MoveNext runs inside the call, but its catch still puts the exception into the task.

cards.q: Inside an async Task method, an exception is thrown after an await. What does the generated code do with it?
options: Calls builder.SetException: the task becomes Faulted and await will throw the exception
Throws it on the thread that ran the continuation and crashes the process
Swallows it: the task completes successfully
cards.explain: The catch in MoveNext hands the exception to the builder, and it waits in the task for whoever awaits it.

cards.q: var t = ParseAsync(""); — the method throws ArgumentException before its first await. What does the caller get on this line?
options: A task in the Faulted state; the exception is thrown at await t
The exception, right on this line
A task that never completes
cards.explain: The first MoveNext runs synchronously, but its catch calls SetException. An exception never escapes the call of an async Task method.

cards.title: ExecutionContext travels with await
cards.body: Along with the continuation, .NET carries the ExecutionContext: the current culture, AsyncLocal<T> values and other "ambient" data of the operation. The context is captured at the pause and restored before the continuation runs, on whatever thread that is. That's why AsyncLocal is visible after await even when another thread runs the continuation.

cards.q: What does Log print after the await?
options: req-42
null
It depends on which thread runs the continuation
cards.explain: ExecutionContext carried the AsyncLocal value along with the continuation, so the thread doesn't matter.

cards.title: ThreadStatic vs. AsyncLocal
cards.body: A [ThreadStatic] field belongs to a thread, not to an operation. If another thread continues the code after await, you read that thread's value. It's either null or, worse, the value of another request that ran on this pool thread earlier. For per-request or per-operation data, use AsyncLocal.
cards.deep: A change to AsyncLocal inside a called async method isn't visible to the caller after it returns: ExecutionContext is immutable and copied on write. The value flows down the call chain, not up.

cards.q: An ASP.NET Core server. At the start of a request a [ThreadStatic] field is set: _user = "ann". Then comes an await on a database query, then Log(_user). What can Log print?
options: Any of the three: ann, null or another request's user name, depending on which pool thread resumes
Always ann: the value was written in this same request
Always null: the field is cleared after await
cards.explain: Any pool thread may run the continuation, and [ThreadStatic] holds whatever that thread's last user wrote into it.

cards.q: What travels across await with the ExecutionContext? Select all that apply.
options: AsyncLocal values
The current culture (CultureInfo.CurrentCulture)
Values of [ThreadStatic] fields
The thread number (Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId)
cards.explain: ThreadStatic and the thread number belong to the thread, not the operation, so they don't travel across await.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Creates and completes the method's task
A container of ambient data carried across await
A single value tied to a logical operation
Per-thread data, lost when the thread changes

units.title: Context and deadlock
units.blurb: SynchronizationContext, the classic .Result deadlock, ConfigureAwait(false), async all the way and thread-pool starvation.

lessons.title: SynchronizationContext
lessons.sub: Who runs the code after await

cards.title: Where code resumes after await
cards.body:
SynchronizationContext is an object with a Post(callback) method: "run this where it belongs". A thread's current context lives in SynchronizationContext.Current.

  • WPF has DispatcherSynchronizationContext, WinForms has WindowsFormsSynchronizationContext: Post puts the callback into the UI thread's message queue.
  • Unity has UnitySynchronizationContext: Post puts the callback into a queue that the main thread drains every frame.
  • A console app and ASP.NET Core: Current == null. Pool threads have no context either, even if Task.Run was called from a window.

cards.title: What await does with the context
cards.body:
At the pause, await reads SynchronizationContext.Current and remembers it.

If there is a context, then when the task completes the continuation is sent there with Post and runs on the UI thread. That's why a handler can touch controls after await: from any other thread, WPF would throw InvalidOperationException.

If there is no context, the continuation runs on a pool thread.

cards.task: Run the scenario in WPF, then switch to a console app and see who runs the continuations.

cards.q: Why can a WPF handler write label.Text = … after await?
options: await captured the UI thread's context, and the continuation arrived there via Post
WPF lets you change controls from any thread
await blocks the UI thread until the response, so the code never leaves it
cards.explain: At the await, SynchronizationContext.Current is a DispatcherSynchronizationContext. The continuation went to the UI thread's queue and ran there.

cards.q: Where does the main thread have a SynchronizationContext by default? Select all that apply.
options: WPF
WinForms
Unity
A console app
ASP.NET Core
cards.explain: In a console app and ASP.NET Core, SynchronizationContext.Current == null, so the pool runs the continuations.

cards.title: A context is a queue
cards.body:
Post runs nothing by itself: it only puts the callback into a queue. The UI thread has one queue for everything (clicks, repaints, continuations after await), and the UI thread works through it one item at a time.

If the UI thread is busy with a long computation or blocked, the queue stalls: neither clicks nor continuations run.

cards.q: The UI thread is busy with a long computation, and a continuation after await is already in its queue. When will it run?
options: When the UI thread finishes the computation and reaches it in the queue
Right away, on a free pool thread
Never: the queue gets dropped
cards.explain: The continuation waits its turn, just like clicks: only the UI thread can run it.

cards.title: When there is no context
cards.body:
If SynchronizationContext.Current == null, await also checks the current TaskScheduler. By default that's the thread pool.

More precisely: without a context the continuation usually runs synchronously on the thread that completed the task, for example the pool thread that got the OS notification that the response arrived. If it can't run right away (for instance, the task has the RunContinuationsAsynchronously flag), it goes into the pool's queue.
cards.deep: SynchronizationContext.Current and TaskScheduler.Current are checked at the moment of the await. You install your own context with SynchronizationContext.SetSynchronizationContext; that's how Unity and libraries such as AsyncContext from Nito.AsyncEx run every continuation on a single thread.

cards.q: In a WPF handler: await Task.Run(async () => { await LoadAsync(); label.Text = "ok"; }); What happens on the label.Text line?
options: InvalidOperationException: there's no context inside Task.Run, so a pool thread runs the continuation
It's fine: Task.Run was started from the UI thread, so await returns there
A deadlock
cards.explain: The await inside the lambda reads the pool thread's SynchronizationContext.Current, which is null. The handler's context doesn't matter here: only the outer await would capture it.

cards.q: Match each environment to its SynchronizationContext
How does ExecutionContext differ from SynchronizationContext?
options: ExecutionContext is data (AsyncLocal, culture) that rides with the continuation; SynchronizationContext is where the continuation itself is sent
They're the same thing under two names
ExecutionContext decides which thread resumes, and SynchronizationContext carries AsyncLocal
cards.explain: ExecutionContext is always captured and restored. SynchronizationContext only decides who runs the continuation: the UI thread via Post, or the pool.

lessons.title: Deadlock with .Result
lessons.sub: The classic UI deadlock

cards.title: A classic
cards.body:
A button handler waits synchronously for an async method. Here's what happens step by step (the numbers are in the code below):

  • 1. The UI thread calls GetDataAsync. The method sends the request synchronously and, at the await, captures the UI thread's context: SynchronizationContext.Current is a DispatcherSynchronizationContext.
  • 2. GetDataAsync returns an unfinished task, and the UI thread blocks on .Result.
  • 3. The response arrives. The continuation (Parse and return) is sent via Post to the UI thread's queue.
  • 4. But the UI thread is stuck on .Result and doesn't process its queue. The continuation won't run until the UI thread is free, and the UI thread won't be free until the task completes.

Each waits for the other: a deadlock. It can happen in any context that lets in only one thread at a time: WPF, WinForms, Unity and classic ASP.NET on .NET Framework (AspNetSynchronizationContext). ASP.NET Core and console apps have no context, so the loop never closes.

cards.task: Switch the handler to .Result and drive the program into a hang.

cards.q: WPF: the UI thread called GetDataAsync().Result, and the server's response has already arrived. What is the UI thread waiting for now?
options: For the GetDataAsync task to complete
For the server's response
For a user click
cards.explain: .Result blocks the thread until the task completes. The response is here, but the task isn't complete yet: its continuation hasn't run.

cards.q: Same scenario: the UI thread is stuck on .Result, and the server's response has arrived. What is the GetDataAsync task waiting for now?
options: For the UI thread to run its continuation from the UI queue
For the server's response
For the thread pool to give it a free thread
cards.explain: await captured the UI context, so the continuation went to the UI thread's queue. Only the UI thread can run it, and it's blocked.

cards.task: Keep .Result, but move the code to a console app. Will it hang?

cards.q: Why doesn't the same .Result hang in a console app?
options: There's no context: a pool thread runs the continuation, not the blocked main thread
A console app runs code faster
In a console app .Result doesn't block the thread
cards.explain: SynchronizationContext.Current == null, so await captured nothing, and the continuation doesn't need the thread that's stuck on .Result.

cards.title: Why it's still bad
cards.body:
In a console app or ASP.NET Core, .Result won't hang, but the thread still sits idle while it waits. On a server that's a pool thread, and under load such threads run out: that's thread-pool starvation, lesson 5.

Blocking on async code is bad everywhere: in a UI it's a deadlock, on a server it's starvation.

cards.q: WPF, the handler calls GetDataAsync().Result, and the server answers after one second. Put the events in order.
items: GetDataAsync sends the request and, at the await, captures the UI context
GetDataAsync returns an unfinished task, and the UI thread blocks on .Result
A second later the response arrives, and the continuation is sent via Post to the UI thread's queue
The continuation never runs: the UI thread is stuck on .Result, a deadlock
cards.explain: The chain closes at the last step: the task needs the UI thread, and the UI thread is waiting for the task.

cards.q: Where can this deadlock happen? Select all that apply.
options: WPF
Unity
Classic ASP.NET on .NET Framework
ASP.NET Core
A console app
cards.explain: You need a context that lets in only one thread at a time: Dispatcher, UnitySynchronizationContext, AspNetSynchronizationContext. ASP.NET Core and console apps have no context.

lessons.title: ConfigureAwait(false)
lessons.sub: Skipping the context, and when that's dangerous

cards.title: Don't go back to the context
cards.body:
ConfigureAwait(false) tells await: "don't capture the SynchronizationContext". The continuation won't go via Post to the UI thread's queue; it runs on a pool thread instead. ExecutionContext is unaffected: AsyncLocal and culture flow as usual.

For library code that doesn't need the UI thread this is the right call: fewer switches, and no deadlock if someone outside calls .Result. Step by step, with an outer .Result in WPF:

  • 1. await doesn't capture the context, and the UI thread blocks on .Result.
  • 2. The response arrives, and a pool thread runs the continuation.
  • 3. The task completes without the UI thread.
  • 4. .Result on the UI thread gets the result. The UI thread itself was stuck the whole time.

cards.task: The code with .Result hangs. Fix it inside the library without touching the handler.

cards.q: WPF: the handler calls GetDataAsync().Result, and ConfigureAwait(false) was added to the await in the library. The deadlock is gone. What changed?
options: A pool thread ran the continuation, and the task completed without the UI thread
The UI thread stopped blocking on .Result
The network started answering faster
cards.explain: The UI thread was still stuck on .Result, but the task no longer needed it.

cards.task: Now the method updates a window control after await. What happens with ConfigureAwait(false)?

cards.q: WPF: after await http.GetStringAsync(url).ConfigureAwait(false) the method writes label.Text = json. Why does it throw?
options: After ConfigureAwait(false) the code ran on a pool thread, and controls can only be touched from the UI thread
ConfigureAwait(false) is forbidden in WPF
The network returned an error
cards.explain: ConfigureAwait(false) only fits where you don't need the UI thread after the await.

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
In libraries, ConfigureAwait(false) on every await. In app code that touches the UI or the Unity API after await, leave it out.

But ConfigureAwait is a safety net, not a cure. The thread on .Result is still stuck. The real cure for the deadlock is not to block at all: next lesson.
cards.deep: .NET 8 added ConfigureAwaitOptions: for example, await task.ConfigureAwait(ConfigureAwaitOptions.SuppressThrowing) waits for the task without throwing. SuppressThrowing is supported only for a Task with no result: for Task<T> it's an error (the CA2261 analyzer, and ArgumentOutOfRangeException at run time). ASP.NET Core has no context, so there ConfigureAwait(false) changes nothing in app code.

cards.q: Where does ConfigureAwait(false) belong? Select all that apply.
options: In an HTTP client library
In a data access library
In a button handler that then changes label.Text
In a Unity script that then moves a transform
cards.explain: Where the code touches the UI or the Unity API after await, it needs the main thread's context.

cards.title: ConfigureAwait only matters on a pause
cards.body:
ConfigureAwait(false) only decides where to send the continuation after a pause. If the task has already completed (a cache hit, the fast path), await doesn't stop, and the code keeps going on the same thread, which is still the UI thread.

The next await without ConfigureAwait(false) reads SynchronizationContext.Current again, captures the UI context, and the deadlock with an outer .Result is back. That's why ConfigureAwait(false) goes on every await, not just "at the start of the method".
cards.code:
var a = await cache.GetAsync(k).ConfigureAwait(false); // cache hit: still the UI thread
var b = await http.GetStringAsync(url);                // captures the UI context → deadlock risk

cards.q: In a library, ConfigureAwait(false) is only on the method's first await, not on the second. Outside, the method is called via .Result from the UI thread. What's the risk?
options: If the first task completed right away, the code stayed on the UI thread, and the second await captures the UI context again
None: after the first ConfigureAwait(false) the method is already running on the pool
A compile error
cards.explain: Without a pause ConfigureAwait(false) has no effect: the thread doesn't change, and the second await sees the UI context.

cards.q: Does ConfigureAwait(false) stop AsyncLocal from flowing?
options: No: it's about SynchronizationContext, while ExecutionContext always flows
Yes: without the context AsyncLocal is lost
Only in a console app
cards.explain: These are two independent mechanisms: SynchronizationContext decides who runs the continuation, ExecutionContext decides what data rides with it.

lessons.title: Async all the way
lessons.sub: How to really cure a deadlock

cards.title: Don't mix them
cards.body:
If the inside is asynchronous, the outside should await too, all the way up to the event handler or Main. That's async all the way. Waiting for a task synchronously (.Result, .Wait(), GetAwaiter().GetResult()) is called sync-over-async: in a UI it gives you a deadlock, on a server it gives you thread-pool starvation.

Why await cures the deadlock (the "after" code below):

  • 1. The await in the handler sees an unfinished task and returns control, so the UI thread is free and keeps running its queue.
  • 2. The response arrives, GetDataAsync's continuation comes via Post into the queue, and the UI thread runs it.
  • 3. The GetDataAsync task completes, the handler's continuation joins the queue, and label.Text changes on the UI thread.

No thread is blocked, so there's no waiting loop.
cards.deep: If the caller can't be async (a constructor, Dispose, a synchronous interface): a static async Task<T> CreateAsync() factory, IAsyncDisposable, an async version of the interface. If there's truly no way around blocking: GetAwaiter().GetResult() with ConfigureAwait(false) along the whole chain, and only off the UI thread.

cards.task: Fix the deadlock properly: no ConfigureAwait, just make the handler async.

cards.q: Why is await better than .Result in a WPF handler?
options: The UI thread isn't blocked: continuations and clicks run, and no waiting loop forms
The code is shorter, the behavior is the same
With await the network answers faster
cards.explain: No blocked thread, no waiting loop.

cards.title: async Main and async handlers
cards.body: Since C# 7.1, Main can be async Task Main(). Event handlers are async void: the one sensible place for void. ASP.NET Core controllers return Task<IActionResult>.
cards.deep: async Task Main is a generated Main that calls Main().GetAwaiter().GetResult(). The console's main thread really does block, and that's fine: there's no context, so the pool runs the continuations.

cards.q: Where is the sync-over-async?
cards.explain: .Result holds a pool thread for the entire database query.

cards.q: Fix the controller
cards.explain: async in the declaration, await before the call.

cards.title: The reverse problem: async-over-sync
cards.body:
Wrapping a blocking synchronous call or a long computation in Task.Run and calling the method …Async is a lie. A thread is still busy, just a different one: a pool thread. On a server that's an extra switch and a pool thread tied up under the guise of asynchrony.

A truly asynchronous method waits without a thread (I/O through the OS). If there's no such API, the library exposes an honest synchronous method, and the caller decides whether Task.Run is needed: yes in a UI, to keep the window from freezing; no on a server.
cards.deep: Files are subtler: on Linux, .NET performs asynchronous reads of regular files on pool threads, because the OS has no convenient async API for them. But that's the platform's doing, not your library's; for sockets and networking, thread-free waiting exists everywhere.

cards.q: In a library: public Task<byte[]> HashAsync(byte[] d) => Task.Run(() => SHA256.HashData(d)); What's wrong?
options: The method ties up a pool thread while posing as asynchronous; whether to use Task.Run is the caller's call
Nothing: Task.Run makes the method truly asynchronous
Task.Run can't be called inside a library; it's a compile error
cards.explain: The computation still occupies a thread, just a pool thread. In a UI the caller will wrap the synchronous HashData in Task.Run itself, and on a server it doesn't need the extra switch.

cards.q: Which of these are sync-over-async? Select all that apply.
options: task.Result
task.Wait()
task.GetAwaiter().GetResult()
await task
await Task.WhenAll(tasks)
cards.explain: Any synchronous wait on a task blocks the thread. GetAwaiter().GetResult() only throws the exception without the AggregateException wrapper; it blocks just the same.

lessons.title: Thread-pool starvation
lessons.sub: The server doesn't crash, it crawls

cards.title: How the pool grows
cards.body:
ASP.NET Core has no context, so .Result won't hang. But every such request holds a pool thread while it waits for the database. How much that hurts depends on how the pool adds threads:

  • up to the MinThreads threshold (by default, the number of cores) the pool creates threads immediately, on demand;
  • beyond the threshold, cautiously. If a thread is blocked by something the pool can't see (Thread.Sleep, synchronous I/O, lock), the pool checks every half second whether the queue is moving and adds one thread at a time;
  • blocking on .Result and .Wait() the pool notices by itself since .NET 6: it immediately adds as many extra threads as there are cores, and after that waits before each new one, from 25 ms up to 250 ms.

You can raise the threshold with ThreadPool.SetMinThreads.
cards.deep: Beyond MinThreads, the thread count is tuned by the hill-climbing algorithm: it tries slightly more or slightly fewer threads and watches whether throughput improves. The half-second check is a safety net for when the queue stalls. Blocking behavior is tunable through the System.Threading.ThreadPool.Blocking.* settings in runtimeconfig.json.

cards.title: A server that crawls
cards.body:
Step by step: 8 cores, 100 requests with .Result arrive.

  • 1. 8 threads take 8 requests and block on .Result. The pool sees the blocking and immediately adds 8 more, which take the next requests and block too. The other 84 wait in the pool's queue.
  • 2. The database responses arrive. But the continuations that the blocked threads need go into the same queue, behind the new requests.
  • 3. New threads now arrive with delays, and a new thread often picks up not a continuation but the next request, which blocks on .Result as well.
  • 4. There are dozens of threads now, responses stretch to seconds, and the CPU is almost idle.

If the blocking comes from Thread.Sleep or a synchronous read instead of .Result, the pool doesn't see it and adds threads even more slowly, one every half second.

cards.task: Add 16 requests with .Result and start the clock. How many threads are stuck, and how does the pool grow?
Now the same 16 requests, but with await.

cards.q: 16 requests with .Result bloated the pool, while the same 16 requests with await were served by 4 threads. Why?
options: With .Result a thread is stuck for the whole database wait; with await it's free while we wait and takes the next piece of work
With await the database answers faster
The pool knew in advance the requests were asynchronous and decided not to add threads
cards.explain: Waiting without a thread is the main benefit of async on a server. The pool doesn't need more threads because none of them is stuck.

cards.q: Under load, responses lag by seconds while the CPU is nearly idle. What do you suspect first?
options: Thread-pool starvation: a .Result or .Wait() somewhere
A slow disk
Too much memory
cards.explain: An idle CPU with growing latency means the threads exist, but they're stuck.

cards.title: How to find it
cards.body: In dotnet-counters, watch the pool's queue length and its thread count. A growing queue and a thread count that creeps upward while CPU load stays low is a sure sign.
cards.deep: On .NET 8 these are the ThreadPool Queue Length and ThreadPool Thread Count counters; since .NET 9, the dotnet.thread_pool.queue.length and dotnet.thread_pool.thread.count metrics. In a process dump (dotnet-dump), starvation shows up as dozens or hundreds of threads whose stacks end in .Result or Wait.
cards.code: dotnet-counters monitor -n MyServer --counters System.Runtime

cards.q: What can cause thread-pool starvation? Select all that apply.
options: .Result and .Wait() on tasks that query the database
Thread.Sleep in code that runs on the pool
A synchronous read from a slow disk in every request
await httpClient.GetAsync(…)
Short computations with no waiting
cards.explain: Anything that holds a pool thread without doing work.

cards.q: A quick "fix": ThreadPool.SetMinThreads(500, 500). What do you say?
options: It hides the symptom: more threads at once, but they sit idle just the same; the cure is switching to await
Great fix: blocking costs nothing anymore
It will speed up the database
cards.explain: The MinThreads threshold removes the delay in growing the pool, not the blocking. Hundreds of waiting threads mean memory and context switches. The real cure is not to block.

lessons.title: Final: context and deadlock
lessons.sub: Hang the program, then fix it three ways

cards.task: Drive the WPF app into a deadlock.
Fix it the right way: no ConfigureAwait, and stay in WPF.

cards.q: Which fix is a safety net rather than a cure?
options: ConfigureAwait(false) in the library
await instead of .Result
Both are a full cure
cards.explain: The thread still blocks on .Result; the deadlock loop just never closes.

cards.q: Where do you need the captured context after await? Select all that apply.
options: A WPF handler updates label.Text
A Unity script moves a transform
A library parses JSON
An ASP.NET Core controller reads the database
cards.explain: A library or a server doesn't need the UI thread.

cards.q: Which line can hang a WPF app?
cards.explain: .Result on the UI thread while SaveAsync awaits inside without ConfigureAwait(false).

cards.q: Why doesn't the same line hang an ASP.NET Core server?
options: There's no context, so the pool runs the continuation; but the thread still sits idle
ASP.NET Core forbids .Result
It uses a different C#
cards.explain: Instead of a deadlock you get thread-pool starvation under load.

cards.q: A WPF OnSave handler calls _service.SaveAsync(doc).Result. Inside SaveAsync there's an await on a request without ConfigureAwait(false), and the server answers after one second. Put the events in order.
items: SaveAsync sends the request and, at the await, captures the UI context
SaveAsync returns an unfinished task, and the UI thread blocks on .Result
A second later the response arrives, and SaveAsync's continuation is sent via Post to the UI thread's queue
The continuation never runs: the UI thread is stuck on .Result, a deadlock
cards.explain: The task needs the UI thread to run its continuation, and the UI thread is waiting for the task. Status.Text never changes.

cards.q: Match them up
